title: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess
hook: Durga meets the buffalo demon; nine nights of dancing, and on the tenth day the good wins

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ganesh Chaturthi. A clay guest welcomed home and given back to the water. Your line was welcome it, then let it go. Did you let one good moment end gently? Day six hundred seventy-two.

The gods have lost. Not a skirmish: the whole war. A demon king named Mahisha, who can take the shape of a buffalo, has beaten them, thrown them out of heaven, and taken their seats. They go, humiliated, to Vishnu and Shiva and tell them everything. And as they tell it, something happens that nobody plans. Their anger starts to glow. That's how the Devi Mahatmya, the great text of the Goddess, opens its most famous battle.
screen: `THE GODS HAVE LOST.` → `MAHISHA TAKES HEAVEN.` → `THEIR ANGER STARTS TO GLOW.`

segments.voice: From the faces of Vishnu and Shiva and Brahma, and then from all the gods, a great light pours out, the text calls it tejas, radiance, and it gathers into one blaze like a mountain on fire. The blaze takes the form of a woman. The Goddess. Every god then gives her something: Shiva a trident, Vishnu a discus, the mountain Himalaya a lion to ride. She laughs, and the sound shakes the worlds. Then she goes to war with Mahisha. He fights her as a buffalo, then a lion, then a man with a sword, then an elephant, then a buffalo again. She pins him under her foot, and as he tries to escape out of the buffalo's mouth in his true form, she ends him. In the Devi Mahatmya, that's one battle among several; she fights for the gods again and again. Navaratri means nine nights: nava, nine, ratri, night. For nine nights in autumn, in the month of Ashvin, many Hindus honor the Goddess, and how they do it changes as you cross India. In Gujarat, whole towns dance garba and dandiya in circles until late. In Bengal, it's Durga Puja, with huge clay images of Durga killing the buffalo demon. In much of the South, families set up golu, steps of dolls. On the tenth day, Vijayadashami, the day of victory, the good has won. And this week ends here, after six days of hard endings and new beginnings: the earth opening, a poem argued over, a midnight birth, a clay guest, and now nine nights, and the dawn.
screen: `THE GODS' RADIANCE BECOMES ONE.` · `THE GODDESS, ARMED BY ALL.` · `MAHISHA CHANGES SHAPE; SHE WINS.` · `NAVA RATRI: NINE NIGHTS.` · then, large: `ON THE TENTH DAY, VICTORY.`

segments.voice: Sit up a little taller and let the breath settle. Think of one small thing that keeps winning in you lately: a bad habit, a sharp word, scrolling past midnight. Name it, silently, once. Then, as you breathe, say inwardly: not tonight. Not as a battle, just a quiet decision. Keep the breath steady, and let the decision rest in the body. The bell holds the time.
Navaratri. Nine nights of the Goddess in autumn, remembering how she defeated Mahisha, and ending on the tenth day, the day of victory.
Your line: nine nights, then the dawn. Tonight, refuse one small thing that's been winning, just for tonight. Day six hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: During autumn Navaratri, many Hindus honor the Goddess for nine nights with fasting, recitation of the Devi Mahatmya, garba and dandiya dancing in Gujarat, Durga Puja in Bengal, and golu doll displays in the South, ending with Vijayadashami on the tenth day.

fork.setup: you're one of the gods, beaten and thrown out of heaven by Mahisha. what happens next, in the text?
options: each god fights him again alone.
the gods hide and wait him out.
their radiance joins and becomes the Goddess.
fork.reveal: their anger becomes light, the light becomes one, and the Goddess rises from it, armed by all of them.

original.note: Sanskrit nava (nine) + rātri (night): the nine nights of the Goddess.

trapdoor: what you thought: Navaratri is a dance festival.
what it means: it's nine nights honoring the Goddess, ending in a day of victory, with dancing in some regions.
what a scholar hears: the Devi Mahatmya, part of the Markandeya Purana, tells Mahisha's defeat in its second and third chapters, and is widely recited during Navaratri.

sources.ref: Devi Mahatmya (Markandeya Purana), chapters 2–3 (the Goddess formed from the gods' radiance; the slaying of Mahisha)
Navaratri practice: garba, Durga Puja, golu (regional practice)

notes: Confirm the order of Mahisha's shapes in Devi Mahatmya chapter 3, and the gifts (Shiva's trident, Vishnu's discus, Himalaya's lion).
There are two main Navaratris (spring Chaitra and autumn Sharada); the script describes the autumn one in Ashvin.
In some tellings Vijayadashami is linked with Rama's victory over Ravana as well; that angle is left for a later Navaratri day.
